# nish/term-rate

how fast the link to the terminal is, measured from frames sent and acknowledged, and the frame rate and drawing detail a program keeps to under it.

```ts
import {
  BACKEND_CAP_ASCII,
  BACKEND_CAP_HALFBLOCK,
  BACKEND_CAP_KITTY,
  BACKEND_CAP_SIXEL,
  CORNER_BOTTOM_LEFT,
  CORNER_BOTTOM_RIGHT,
  CORNER_TOP_LEFT,
  CORNER_TOP_RIGHT,
  DETAIL_FIRST,
  RATE_FIRST,
  RateController,
  RateDecision,
  RateOptions,
  TermStats,
  drawStatsOverlay,
} from "nish/term-rate";
```

<scalar-callout type="info">

The module is pure: no capability, no I/O and no clock. The caller feeds a
`RateController` what happened — a frame of so many bytes, costing so many
nanoseconds to build, sent at a time; an acknowledgement arriving at a time —
and asks it whether a frame may be drawn now and in what shape
(`RateDecision`). Every time is an `f64` count of milliseconds on the
caller's clock, as `FixedStep`'s is in `nish/term`.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="The acknowledgement">

A frame is acknowledged when the terminal answers a
status query sent right after it: the terminal answers in order, so the
answer means every byte before it has been read and drawn. The query to send
is DSR 5, `CSI 5 n`, answered `CSI 0 n`. It is preferred over the cursor
position report (DSR 6, `CSI 6 n`, answered `CSI row ; col R`) because its
answer is one fixed string, and because a cursor report is the same bytes as
F3 with modifiers in the legacy key encoding (`CSI 1 ; mods R`), which a key
decoder would have to guess between. Two relays answer the query from their
own emulator, not from the terminal at the end of the link:

- tmux (commit 939e8e65) answers in `input.c` lines 1737–1747, the
  `INPUT_CSI_DSR` case, which replies `\033[0n` to 5 and the position to 6
  through `input_reply`, whose `input_send_reply` (lines 1177–1186) writes to
  the pane. Inside tmux the round trip measures tmux, not the outer
  terminal, and a frame tmux has taken is not yet on the screen.
- mosh (commit decd9b70) answers in `src/terminal/terminalfunctions.cc`
  lines 471–488, `CSI_DSR`, which appends the reply to `terminal_to_host`;
  `src/frontend/mosh-server.cc` feeds the program's output to that emulator
  at line 874 and writes `terminal_to_host` back to the program at line 882.
  The answer comes from mosh-server on the remote host and never crosses the
  network, so mosh reads as a fast local link; its own frame rate limit
  (mosh sends at most about 50 frames a second) then does the pacing.

</scalar-detail>

Under either relay the controller still bounds the program to what the relay
absorbs, which is the most it can know.

<scalar-detail title="What is measured">

Four running averages (exponentially weighted, so
recent frames count most and none is stored): the round trip from a frame's
send to its acknowledgement (weight 1/8, as TCP smooths its round trip, so
one late answer moves it little); the bytes a second the link delivered;
the cost to build a frame and the bytes in one (weight 1/4 each, so a
change of scene shows within a few frames).
The bandwidth and the latency are kept apart, so neither can take the
other's share of a round trip. A frame sent before the previous answer, and
answered more than the latency after it, kept the link busy from that answer
to its own: its bytes over that time measure the bandwidth. A frame sent
onto an idle link makes a trip, kept with the last 16 and the probe's:
against the quickest kept trip, one twice its bytes or half, 2 ms or more
apart, measures the bandwidth from the difference, which the latency is no
part of.
Both kinds smooth the bytes and the time apart (weight 1/4 each), so answers
arriving in a burst, each taking almost no time, do not read as unbounded
bandwidth; answers under 2 ms apart measure nothing this way. A sample
counts for the decisions for 5 seconds with no newer one, so a link that
narrows is not held to its old rate; the bandwidth reported keeps it until
a newer sample, which starts the average afresh, replaces it, or three
trips in a row take over twice what it and the quickest trip kept when
it was taken predict. The figure
is at least the most of the last 16 answers' bytes over their whole round
trips, since the bytes took no longer than that, so a link that widens shows on its first quick answer; but that
bound counts the latency as bytes' time, so alone it never makes the
bandwidth known to the decisions. The base latency is the least, over the
kept trips, of the round trip less the trip's bytes at the bandwidth: the
probe's round trip (`probeRttMs`: the status query alone is a few bytes, so
its round trip is the latency) counts from the start, the frames' once the
bandwidth is known. The kept trips roll over, so a changed route shows
within 16 trips. With frames of one size sent one at a time onto
an idle link and no probe the latency and the bytes cannot be told apart:
the bandwidth is then not known, its load counts as 0, and the trip load
governs on the frame's measured round trip: a cut is taken to shorten none
of it and a restore to lengthen all of it, so detail is neither cut for a
gain nor restored at a cost that may not be there.
Acknowledgements match sent frames oldest first. A frame due while the
unacknowledged limit is reached is dropped and counted; one not answered
within `rateAckTimeoutMs` plus four round trips is given up and counted as
lost, so a lost answer
stalls drawing for seconds, not for ever. Its answer may still come late, and
would otherwise be matched to the next frame, so after a give-up no frame is
drawn until as many answers have arrived, or one more timeout has passed
without them. A time, cost or size that is not a finite number, or is
negative, is not measured, and an empty frame says nothing about bandwidth.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="What is decided">

The frame rate is a tier: 120 (only with `allow120` and
a `maxFps` of 120), 60, 30, 20, 15, 10 or 5. A tier fits when three loads
are all at most 1: the frame cost over 70% of the frame time, the bytes a
second the tier needs over 70% of the bytes a second the link delivers, and
the tier's frames times the round trip over 70% of the time the
unacknowledged limit allows (a link that answers in 100 ms carries at most
ten frames a second one at a time). The 30% left over absorbs a slow frame
without a dropped one. The rate falls to the best fitting tier after half a
second continuously over, and rises one tier after three seconds
continuously under the next tier's loads with a fifth to spare; after any
change it holds for a second, so the averages see the new rate before the
next decision. Falling fast and rising slowly keeps a flickering link from
flipping the rate.

</scalar-detail>

It starts at the best tier on a local terminal: the probe answered under
5 ms, or no `SSH_*` hint and no slow answer. Falling costs half a second and
rising one tier costs three, so a terminal that keeps up is never made to
climb. A probe that took 5 ms or more starts at 30, and a remote session
(the hint, and no fast answer) at 15, as a backlog on a slow link takes far
longer to drain than to avoid.

Below the floor tier (the least tier at or above `minFps`, under
`RATE_FIRST`) the controller cuts bytes instead of frames, one step at a
time: half the resolution, a quarter, the backend capped at half blocks, 256
colours. A step is taken only when it would cut the load by a fifth: a link
whose round trip is all latency is not helped by smaller frames, so it gets a
lower tier at full detail instead. Past the last step, tiers below `minFps`
remain. `DETAIL_FIRST` swaps the order: every tier down to 5 first, then the
steps. Recovery runs the same path backwards with the rising rule, predicting
a step's bytes and cost from the factors in `rateLevelFactor`.

A fixed rate — `fixedFps` from the program or `envFps`, the user's
`NISH_TERM_FPS`, which wins — turns the choosing off: the rate is that one,
at full detail, and only the unacknowledged limit still applies.

## drawStatsOverlay

`screen`: the rate, round trip and kilobytes a second, then the frame cost,
the frames dropped and the backend cap. A screen too small clips them.

function drawStatsOverlay(
  screen: Screen,
  stats: TermStats,

## RateController

The refresh controller. Each turn of a program's loop: feed it the
acknowledgements that arrived (`ackReceived`), let it re-decide (`tick`),
and draw only when `mayDraw` says so, reporting the frame with `frameSent`.
`decision` says how to draw it. `decision` and `stats` answer the same object
each call, updated in place, so a loop allocates nothing.

```ts
class RateController
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new RateController(options: RateOptions)` | A controller for `options`, read once. |
| `ackBusyMs: f64` | The smoothed time the link spent on an answered frame, in milliseconds, for the bandwidth. |
| `ackBytes: f64` | The smoothed bytes of an answered frame, for the bandwidth. |
| `baseRttMs: f64` | The link's latency without bytes: the least, over the kept trips, of the round trip less the bytes' time. |
| `bytesPerSec: f64` | The bytes a second delivered: `ackBytes` over `ackBusyMs`, at least the most of `floorPerSec`, which alone is a lower bound. Samples older than `rateFreshMs` still count here while trips agree with them, but no decision uses them. |
| `changedMs: f64` | When the tier or step last changed. |
| `contradicted: i32` | How many trips in a row have contradicted the aged bandwidth sample. |
| `costMs: f64` | The smoothed frame cost, in milliseconds. |
| `current: RateDecision` |  |
| `dropped: i32` |  |
| `fixedFps: i32` | The fixed frame rate, or 0 when the controller chooses. |
| `floorFps: i32` | The least tier detail is cut to keep: the floor tier under `RATE_FIRST`, 5 under `DETAIL_FIRST`. |
| `floorNext: i32` | Where the next goes in `floorPerSec` once it is full. |
| `floorPerSec: f64[]` | The bytes a second each of the latest answers proves at least, its bytes over its round trip. |
| `frameBytes: f64` | The smoothed bytes per frame. |
| `haveAck: boolean` | Whether a frame has been acknowledged, so decisions can start. |
| `haveFrame: boolean` | Whether a frame has been sent, so cost and size are known. |
| `haveRate: boolean` | Whether the bandwidth is known, so decisions may use it: sampled by a frame that waited behind another or two trips of different sizes, within `rateFreshMs`. The answers' bytes over their round trips are only a lower bound and never make it known. |
| `haveRtt: boolean` | Whether a round trip, from the probe or an answer, is known. |
| `head: i32` | The oldest unacknowledged frame's index in `sentMs`. |
| `heldLatencyMs: f64` | The latency as last worked out while the bandwidth was known, held once its samples age out. |
| `lastAckMs: f64` | When the last acknowledgement arrived, or -1. |
| `level: i32` | The detail step in force, 0 (full detail) to `rateMaxLevel`. |
| `lost: i32` |  |
| `maxUnacked: i32` |  |
| `measured: TermStats` |  |
| `minTier: i32` | The least tier above which `RATE_FIRST` keeps full detail. |
| `overSinceMs: f64` | When the loads went over budget and stayed, or -1. |
| `paced: boolean` | Whether a frame has been asked for, so the pacer's clock runs. |
| `pacer: FixedStep` | Paces frames at `tier`. |
| `prefer: i32` |  |
| `rateAtMs: f64` | When the bandwidth was last sampled, by a frame that waited behind another or by two trips. |
| `rateQuickMs: f64` | The quickest kept trip, or the round trip with none kept, when the bandwidth was last sampled: at least the latency then. |
| `rttMs: f64` | The smoothed round trip, in milliseconds. |
| `sentBytes: i32[]` | Their byte counts. |
| `sentMs: f64[]` | The send times of the unacknowledged frames, oldest at `head`. |
| `stale: i32` | Frames given up on whose answers may still come: the next answers are theirs, and no frame is drawn meanwhile. |
| `staleSinceMs: f64` | When frames were last given up on, while `stale` waits for their late answers. |
| `tier: i32` | The frame rate in force. |
| `tiers: i32[]` | The tiers allowed, fastest first, ending at 5. |
| `tripBytes: f64[]` | Their byte counts, 0 for the probe. |
| `tripMs: f64[]` | The round trips of the probe and of the latest frames sent onto an idle link, `rateTripCount` at most. |
| `tripNext: i32` | Where the next trip goes in `tripMs` once it is full. |
| `underSinceMs: f64` | When the next step up came within its margin and stayed, or -1. |
| `ackReceived(nowMs: f64): void` | An acknowledgement arrived at `nowMs`; it answers the oldest frame not yet answered. While frames given up on may still be answered, it is theirs, since the terminal answers in order. One with no frame waiting (a stray answer) is ignored, and one whose time is not a finite number answers its frame and measures nothing. |
| `ageRate(nowMs: f64): void` | Stop deciding on the bandwidth once no sample is newer than `rateFreshMs` at `nowMs`. The figure stays in `bytesPerSec` until a sample replaces it or a trip contradicts it. |
| `decide(nowMs: f64): void` | `tick`'s choosing, past its guards. |
| `decision(): RateDecision` | How to draw the next frame, as of the last `tick`. |
| `fasterTier(fps: i32): i32` | The slowest allowed tier faster than `fps`, or `fps` at the top. |
| `fixedPart(rtt: f64, scale: f64): f64` | The part of a round trip of `rtt` that a detail change scaling the bytes by `scale` leaves alone: the latency once the bandwidth is known. While it is not, the guess is the cautious one each way: less detail shortens no more than the round trip's excess over the quickest trip kept, which is at least the latency, so detail is not cut for a gain that may not be there; more lengthens all of it, so detail is not restored on a link that may not carry it. |
| `frameSent( bytes: i32, costNs: f64, nowMs: f64, ): void` | A frame of `bytes` bytes, which took `costNs` nanoseconds to build, was sent at `nowMs`. A call whose time is not a finite number is ignored; a cost that is not a finite number or is negative is not measured, and negative bytes count as none. |
| `leastLatency(): f64` | The latency: the least, over the kept trips, of the round trip less its bytes' time at the measured bandwidth. While the bandwidth is not known only an empty trip, the probe's, says anything; with none it is the latency held from when the bandwidth was last known, or 0 before that: a lower bound, which is what telling a waited frame from a trip needs, and one that a probe trip rolled out of the kept trips does not drop to 0, or every frame sent before the answer ahead of it would look waited. The bandwidth never comes from the latency on an idle link, so neither can drag the other down. |
| `load(fps: i32, level: i32, nowMs: f64): f64` | The worst of the three loads (cost, bytes, round trip) at `fps` frames a second and detail step `level`, against the 70% budgets: at most 1 fits. A step other than the current one is predicted from the measured frame; `nowMs` lets a frame long unanswered count as a round trip at least that long. A load not yet measured counts as 0. |
| `mayDraw(nowMs: f64): boolean` | Whether a frame may be drawn at `nowMs`: one is due at the tier's pace and fewer than `maxUnacked` frames await their acknowledgement. The first call starts the pace and answers a frame at once. A due frame refused for the limit, or while the answers to frames given up on may still come, is counted as dropped, and the next waits for the next step. A time that is not a finite number is refused. |
| `measureRate(bytes: f64, busyMs: f64): void` | The link spent `busyMs` on `bytes`: one sample of the bandwidth. |
| `measureTrip(rtt: f64, bytes: f64): void` | A frame of `bytes` sent onto an idle link came back in `rtt`: its latency plus its bytes' time, which cannot be told apart alone. Against the quickest trip kept, a frame at least twice the size (or twice as small) whose round trip differs by `rateSplitMs` or more does tell them apart: the extra bytes took the extra time, and the latency drops out. Frames of one size measure nothing here, so small frames cannot drag the bandwidth down to their round trip. |
| `moveTo(fps: i32, level: i32, nowMs: f64): void` | Move to `fps` at detail step `level` at `nowMs`, rescaling the frame averages to the step. |
| `publish(): void` | Copy the state into `current` and `measured`. |
| `slowerTier(fps: i32, least: i32): i32` | The fastest allowed tier slower than `fps` and no slower than `least`, or `least`. |
| `stats(): TermStats` | What has been measured, as of the last `tick`. |
| `stepDown(nowMs: f64): void` | One step down the path at `nowMs`, when over budget: fewer frames, or less detail. |
| `stepUp(): i32` | The next state up the path, as `fps * 8 + level`, or -1 at the top. It is the descent backwards: tiers below the floor first, then detail, then tiers above it. |
| `tick(nowMs: f64): void` | Re-decide at `nowMs`: give up frames long unanswered, then fall, cut detail, restore it or rise, at most one change, with the hysteresis the module header describes. Nothing is decided before the first acknowledgement, nor at a fixed rate. |
| `unacked(): i32` | Frames sent and not yet acknowledged. |
| `updateRate(): void` | The bandwidth: the smoothed samples, but never under what the latest answers prove, so a link that widens, or whose answers are read late, is not taken for a narrow one. Only samples make it known, and only while the latest is within `rateFreshMs` of the latest answer: an answer's bytes over its whole round trip count the latency as bytes' time, and on a far link that reads the bandwidth several times too low. |

## RateDecision

How to draw the next frame: its rate and how much detail.

```ts
class RateDecision
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new RateDecision()` | Full detail at 30 frames a second, until the controller says otherwise. |
| `backendCap: i32` | The richest backend to draw with, a `BACKEND_CAP_*`. |
| `fps: i32` | Frames a second. |
| `palette256: boolean` | Whether to keep to the 256-colour palette. |
| `resolutionDivisor: i32` | Draw at the screen's resolution divided by this: 1, 2 or 4. |

## RateOptions

What a program asks of the controller. Every field has a default, so a program sets only what it means.

```ts
class RateOptions
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new RateOptions()` | The defaults; set the fields to change them. |
| `allow120: boolean` | Whether the 120 tier may be used, for a terminal known to keep up with it. |
| `envFps: i32` | The user's `NISH_TERM_FPS`, which fixes the rate over everything else; 0 when unset. |
| `fixedFps: i32` | A frame rate the program fixes, turning the choosing off; 0 leaves it on. |
| `maxFps: i32` | The most frames a second; 120 is reached only with `allow120` as well. |
| `maxUnacked: i32` | How many frames may be awaiting their acknowledgement at once: 1 or 2. |
| `minFps: i32` | The least frame rate worth keeping before detail is cut, under `RATE_FIRST`. |
| `prefer: i32` | `RATE_FIRST` or `DETAIL_FIRST`: what gives way first when even `minFps` does not fit. |
| `probeRttMs: f64` | The round trip of a probe query sent at startup, in milliseconds; 0 when none was measured. |
| `remoteHint: boolean` | Whether the environment says the terminal is remote (an `SSH_*` variable, say). |

## TermStats

What the controller has measured, for a program to show or log.

```ts
class TermStats
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new TermStats()` | Nothing measured yet. |
| `backend: i32` | The backend cap in force, a `BACKEND_CAP_*`. |
| `bytesPerSec: f64` | The smoothed bytes a second the link delivers. |
| `dropped: i32` | Due frames skipped because the unacknowledged limit was reached. |
| `frameCostMs: f64` | The smoothed cost to build a frame, in milliseconds. |
| `lost: i32` | Frames given up on after waiting `rateAckTimeoutMs` past four round trips. |
| `rttMs: f64` | The smoothed round trip from a frame's send to its acknowledgement, in milliseconds. |
| `tier: i32` | The frame rate in force. |
| `unacked: i32` | Frames sent and not yet acknowledged. |
